extracted.intended_audience: citizens/voters and legislators considering the proposed U.S. Constitution; readers seeking authoritative exposition of the judiciary provisions (e.g., New York electorate, statesmen, legal thinkers)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository argument and guidance on the proper construction and implementation of the federal judiciary under the proposed U.S. Constitution, covering jurisdictional divisions, appeals, trial by jury, judicial independence, and relations between federal and state courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial power limited to enumerated cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The judicial power of the United States shall be vested in one Supreme Court and such inferior courts as Congress shall ordain and establish; the Constitution enumerates the cases to which judicial power extends, and that enumeration marks the precise limits of federal judicial authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specification of particular cases excludes a more general judicial authority; federal courts cannot extend jurisdiction beyond the enumerated objects because to do so would nullify the purpose of specifying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court original jurisdiction narrow and specific
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court will have original jurisdiction only in cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, and those in which a State shall be a party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These classes are rarely to occur and are suited for first-instance determination by the nation's highest judicatory for reasons of public peace and respect to sovereignties; other cases are to originate in inferior tribunals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court appellate jurisdiction extends to law and fact, subject to congressional exceptions/regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court shall possess appellate jurisdiction both as to law and fact in cases referred to it, and that jurisdiction is subject to such exceptions and regulations as Congress shall make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate jurisdiction can cover pure law review and, in certain cases (especially those in the civil-law tradition), re-examination of facts; Congress may regulate the mode and scope (including where fact re-examination is permitted or barred) to preserve justice and practicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate re-examination of facts is procedural and legislatively regulable
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-examination of facts decided by a jury in an inferior court is not necessarily implied by appellate jurisdiction; where permitted, it may be conducted by a second jury, by remanding for retrial, or by issuing an issue for the Supreme Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different state usages (common-law jury practice vs. civil-law modes) counsel a flexible national rule; the new government should let legislation determine whether appeals re-try facts and by what process to avoid abolishing jury trial or imposing uniform modes unsuited to local practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate jurisdiction does not abolish trial by jury
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of appellate jurisdiction 'both as to law and fact' does not imply abolition of the trial by jury in civil or criminal matters; silence on a civil jury clause does not equal prohibition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Constitution expressly requires jury trial in criminal cases but is silent for civil cases; that silence leaves the legislature free to provide for juries in civil causes as it sees fit, and appellate review can be structured to preserve jury functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: State courts retain pre-existing jurisdiction unless exclusively delegated
rubrics_metrics.description: State courts will retain the jurisdiction they now have unless that jurisdiction is taken away by express grant to the Union, by an incompatible duplicate authority, or by explicit prohibition to the States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concurrent jurisdiction in federal matters is the default where no exclusion is expressed; federal and state systems should be treated as parts of one whole, with state tribunals as natural auxiliaries in executing national laws unless Congress clearly provides otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals from state courts to the Supreme Court are within the Constitution's scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution's grant of appellate jurisdiction to the Supreme Court in enumerated cases should be construed to include appeals from state tribunals, because the grant contemplates the objects of appeal (federal causes), not just the inferior federal tribunals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricting appeals to only federal inferior courts would enable evasion of federal authority and frustrate the intent to have national principles uniformly settled; appeals from state courts therefore lie to the Supreme Court unless excluded by law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congress may constitute inferior federal tribunals and define their authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress is empowered to constitute tribunals inferior to the Supreme Court; whether such courts exercise original or appellate jurisdiction (or both) is left largely to legislative discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creating district courts (possibly fewer than one per state, organized into several districts) and using circuit arrangements can make federal justice efficient while allowing Congress to circumscribe appeals and manage the Supreme Court's docket.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage appeals to avoid an 'unrestrained course' of appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: The appellate path should be fashioned so as not to encourage unbridled appeals that would be a source of public and private inconvenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By adjusting appellate routes (e.g., making appeals lie to district courts in some instances, limiting appeals to the Supreme Court), Congress can reduce needless multiplicity of appeals and safeguard efficient administration of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence through tenure and good behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges should hold office during good behavior (life tenure) rather than be selected for limited terms as legislators are, to ensure independence and proficiency in legal knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placing final judicial authority in a body with permanent tenure reduces the likelihood that those who helped pass bad laws will be disposed to interpret them leniently; it avoids subjecting legal judgments to periodic political fluctuation and factional influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vesting final judicial power in a legislative body or part thereof
rubrics_metrics.description: Entrusting ultimate judgment to the legislature, or a part of it, risks bias because those legislators may have participated in making the laws and will lack the specialized legal knowledge and independent disposition expected of judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separation of powers favors distinct, independent judicial bodies rather than legislative branches acting as final courts; using the legislature as a court undermines impartiality and legal competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment as a legislative check on the judiciary
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of instituting impeachments in one legislative chamber and trying them in the other provides an important constitutional check on judicial usurpation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the legislature retains the means to punish judicial presumption (impeachment and removal), the fear of judicial encroachment is mitigated; this check supports confidence in an independent judiciary while deterring abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: State sovereign immunity — states not amenable to suit without consent
rubrics_metrics.description: It is inherent in sovereignty that a State is not amenable to suit by an individual without its consent; contracts with a sovereign bind conscience but do not create compulsive right of action absent surrender of immunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speculations that federal courts could be used to compel states to pay debts by suits are without foundation unless sovereign immunity is surrendered by the state in the constitutional plan or subsequent legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different procedural traditions (common law vs civil law) counsel flexible appellate rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Because some states try causes by jury (common law) and others use civil-law modes, a universal constitutional exception (e.g., excluding cases originally tried by jury) would be impracticable; the Constitution therefore allows appellate jurisdiction broadly, with regulation by Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The government should enable appellate procedures that can accommodate both modes — e.g., allowing remands for a second jury or other legislatively prescribed mechanisms — rather than rigidly forbidding factual re-examination in appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification as an interpretive rule: particular excludes general only when natural
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal maxims like 'the specification of particulars is an exclusion of generals' must be applied with common sense; specifying jury trial for criminal cases does not imply prohibition of jury trials in civil cases unless the context naturally dictates exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional interpretation should favor the natural and obvious sense of provisions over strained technical maxims; context and purpose determine whether a specification excludes a general power.
